title: Build a data URI from an image

seo.metaTitle: PNG to Data URI - Free Embed String, No Upload, No Limits
seo.metaDescription: Turn an image into a complete data:image/png;base64,... value for CSS, HTML or JSON and copy it in one click. Free, no upload, no limits, encoded locally.
seo.longDescription: Build a data URI takes an image and produces the complete string that lets it live inside a text file: the data: prefix, the media type, the base64 marker, a comma and the encoded picture — ready to paste into a background-image declaration, an HTML src attribute, a JSON config or an email template, with a button that copies the whole value. The encoding always produces a PNG, whatever you loaded, because the pixels are re-encoded through a canvas: a JPG or WebP comes back as PNG bytes inside the data URI. Everything runs in your browser.
facts: Encoded entirely in your browser: the image and the string never leave the page.
Complete value with prefix — the payload alone is the Base64 tool.
The output is always image/png, whatever format went in.
Base64 costs about a third more characters than the raw bytes.
Free with no daily limit, no watermark and no account, also for commercial use.
howTo: Drop the image into the source area, or pick a file from your device.
Wait for the full data:image/png;base64,... string to appear in the result panel.
Press the copy button to take the whole value, prefix included.
Paste it into a background-image declaration, a src attribute or a JSON config.

faq.q: How is this different from the Base64 string?
faq.a: The Base64 output is only the payload. The data URI adds the data: prefix, the image/png media type and the comma, which an attribute expects as a whole. The data URI to PNG page here does the reverse.

faq.q: Does it stay a PNG if I upload a JPG?
faq.a: Yes, and that is worth knowing: the pixels are encoded again as a PNG, so the data URI always says image/png and carries PNG data.

faq.q: Why is the string so much longer than the file?
faq.a: Base64 stores six bits per character, so it costs about a third more characters than the raw bytes. It is a transport format, not a compression one.
